metadata.title: Postmarketing Approaches to Obtain Data on Populations Underrepresented in Clinical Trials for Drugs and Biological Products

candidates.statement: FDA regulations require sponsors to present information from premarket clinical trials on the 18 safety and effectiveness of drugs 2 in terms of sex, age, and racial subgroups. 3,4 These clinical 19 trials should include patient populations that are historically underrepresented in clinical research 20 (e.g., populations based on race, ethnicity, sex, or age.) 5 However, if, despite the sponsor’s best 21 efforts, these populations are not adequately represented in premarket clinical trials, it may be 22 appropriate to collect such data in the postmarketing setting. The purpose of this guidance is to 23 describe FDA requirements and provide recommendations for obtaining safety and effectiveness 24 information on drugs, when appropriate, in the postmarketing setting in historically 25 underrepresented patient populations in clinical trials. 26

Efforts should be made, whether in the premarket or postmarketing setting, to include other underrepresented populations including but not limited to, geographic location, sex, socioeconomic status, disability, pregnancy status, lactation status, and co-morbidity.

candidates.statement: The Agency strongly recommends sponsors obtain information from a diverse, representative 65 patient population early in drug development before initial approval but recognizes that in certain 66 circumstances this information may be limited and must be balanced within the benefit-risk 67 framework, including whether there is unmet medical need and the importance of the product 68 within the overall therapeutic armamentarium. 15 Obtaining information early in development 69 can be advantageous in that information about differential pharmacokinetics (PK), 70 pharmacodynamics (PD), efficacy, or safety may help inform subsequent clinical trials and, 71 ultimately, result in more efficient, informative, and successful drug development. However, if 72 despite the sponsor’s best efforts, such information could not be obtained prior to initial approval 73 of a drug, this information can be obtained in the postmarketing setting. 74

candidates.statement: A. Considerations for Single-Arm Trials 142 • Single-arm trials can be designed with a sample size calculation intended to rule out a 143 historical rate of safety or efficacy to help provide assurance that the medical product 144 is safe and effective in the relevant subpopulation(s). 145 • Single-arm trials can use a Bayesian posterior probability model to exclude the 146 historical rate at pre-specified levels, e.g., 90 percent or higher. 147 • Single-arm trial designs can also allow for ‘borrowing’ of patients from the pre- 148 approval study(ies) when appropriate to obtain a larger sample size of the 149 subpopulation of interest. 150 • Single arm trials should collect PK and PD (if applicable) information to inform or 151 understand any differences in the subpopulation of interest detected in the 152 registrational studies. 153 • Single arm trials can enroll and analyze subpopulations underrepresented in the main 154 analysis population in a separate cohort as a parallel arm of the trial. When clinically 155 appropriate, the separate cohort may be opened/closed simultaneously with the main 156 cohort or in an asynchronous manner. In some cases, the separate cohort can be 157 actively accruing at the time of the new drug application (NDA) or biologics license 158 application (BLA) submission. For example, if the separate cohort is evaluating a 159 group at high risk for toxicity, the cohort may open after the primary analysis portion 160 of the trial to obtain more safety information prior to enrollment of the higher risk 161 population. Alternatively, the separate cohort may remain open after the primary 162

candidates.statement: The sponsor’s approach to provide information on underrepresented populations should be 206 discussed with the FDA review division early in a product development program. FDA 207 recommends submission of a diversity plan as outlined in the guidance for industry, Diversity 208 Plans to Improve Enrollment of Participants from Underrepresented Racial and Ethnic 209 Populations in Clinical Trials. 33 , 34 As noted above, the sponsor and FDA should work 210 together to determine appropriate benchmarks for an inclusive and representative data 211 package that is specific to each development plan. If during the course of the clinical 212 development program, the strategies implemented to recruit and retain a representative 213 population appear unlikely to accomplish the intended objective despite best efforts, the 214 sponsor and FDA should discuss next steps. If it is determined that additional information 215 should be collected in the postmarketing period, such data can provide clinically useful 216 information and can potentially be added to drug labeling, when appropriate. 217

candidates.statement: Under 21 CFR 314.106, FDA may approve a marketing application based solely on 232 foreign clinical data if, among other factors, the data are applicable to the U.S. population 233 and U.S. medical practice. If a sponsor submits a marketing application comprised of 234 patients enrolled predominantly outside of the United States, data and rationale should be 235 submitted to support applicability to the U.S. population and medical practice. FDA may 236 request or require studies or trials to further characterize the efficacy or safety of the 237 product in subpopulations relevant to the U.S. population. 238
